heading: Area law and PEPS approximation for gapped two-dimensional ground states
lede: Two manuscripts posted on September 24, 2026 claim proofs of two long-open statements about gapped quantum spin systems on the square lattice, assuming only that the full Hamiltonian has a spectral gap. This page follows the Lean formalization of both proofs.
description: Hourly progress of the Lean formalization of the two-dimensional area law and polynomial PEPS approximation.
label: openai-math

repos.name: TNLean
repos.description: Tensor-network theory in Lean 4: the fundamental theorem of matrix product states, canonical forms, parent Hamiltonians, matrix-product density operators, projected entangled pair states and local circuits.

repos.name: QICLean
repos.description: Quantum information and channels in Lean 4, following Wolf's Quantum Channels & Operations: channel representations, Kadison–Schwarz theory, quantum Perron–Frobenius and spectral theory, GKSL semigroups and entropy.

routes.heading: How the area law is proved
routes.intro: The proof shows that a piece of A shares almost no information with anything beyond a thin collar around it, then cuts A into regions whose entropies cancel. Each stage gives the physical idea, the results it needs, and the state of the formalization.

stages.title: A first bound below volume
stages.physics: The ground state Ω is separated from all other energies by a gap. Because of the gap, the eigenvalues of a region's reduced state fluctuate little on a log scale. The reason is simple. Reweighting Ω inside the region costs energy only where terms cross its boundary. Next, surround a small box with nested regions, and put a positive operator, a filter, on each. Choose the filters to make the norm {{tn:al-filter-norm}} as large as possible. Here L1, …, Lm are the filters, from the smallest region to the largest. The proof bounds this best norm from above and from below. Comparing the two bounds discounts the box's entropy. Given a surrounding buffer, the box keeps at most half its entropy, plus a constant times its side. Averaging this over many small boxes in random order gives the bound below.
stages.delivers: Take a box of side r far from the cut. Its entropy obeys S ≤ C r1+e₀. Here C is a constant and e₀ is a fixed number below 1. The trivial volume bound grows like r².
stages.caption: Entropy bounds for a box of side r, on log–log axes. Each power of r becomes a straight line. The trivial volume bound has slope 2. This stage gives slope 1 + e₀, with e₀ a fixed number below 1 (drawn at ½). The dashed line of slope 1 is the area law, which later stages reach.

diagrams.caption: Sites of the lattice near a box Q0 far from the cut. The cut splits the lattice into a region A and the rest. The target X is the part of A inside Q0. The nested regions X1 ⊂ X2 are the parts of A inside larger and larger boxes around Q0. A positive operator, the filter Lj, acts on each Xj. The shells around X form the buffer.

Proof of Lemma 3.1, as a tensor diagram. Ψ is a gapped ground state, and ρ is its reduced state on a block B. Multiply Ψ on B by F = ρ−u/2, for a small number u. Then trace out everything outside B, which is the joined leg. The result is σ = ρ1−u/M(u), where M(u) = Tr ρ1−u normalizes it. Only terms crossing the boundary of B feel F. So the reweighted state costs little energy, and the gap keeps it close to Ψ. This limits how far −log pj strays from the entropy, where pj are the eigenvalues of ρ.

From Section 3. Ω is the ground state. Positive operators L1, …, Lm act on nested regions X1 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Xm around a target X. The diagram is the norm N = ‖Lm⋯L1Ω‖, drawn for m = 2. The shells are T1 = X1 ∖ X and T2 = X2 ∖ X1. The leg Λ ∖ X2 is every other site. Bounding −2 log N from above and from below bounds the entropy of X given its shells.

stages.title: Make the Hamiltonian local and positive
stages.physics: The Hamiltonian H is replaced by a sum of positive pieces ki, one per interaction term. Each piece annihilates the ground state Ω: {{tn:al-kill}}. Each piece acts mostly near its own term. Its tail decays faster than any power of the distance. Two tools give this. One is a Lieb–Robinson bound in the lattice's own graph distance. The other is a smooth filter in energy whose Fourier transform decays stretched-exponentially.
stages.delivers: Positive operators ki, one per interaction term. Each annihilates the ground state Ω and has a rapidly decaying spatial tail. Their sum is at least a constant times H − E0, where E0 is the ground energy. So the sum keeps a gap.
stages.caption: Left: the spectrum of H as a rug, with the ground energy E0 and the gap Δ above it. The filter χ is a smooth bump in energy. It equals 1 at E0 and vanishes on every excited energy. Right: the size of its Fourier transform at time t, on a log scale. Its tail falls below every power law. This keeps each piece concentrated near its interaction term.

diagrams.caption: Section 4, read left to right. H is the Hamiltonian, Ω its ground state and E0 its ground energy. Take one interaction term hi, acting on sites Xi. Evolve it for time t and average over t with a smooth weight f. The Fourier transform χ of f equals 1 at zero and vanishes at every excitation energy. Subtract the number ⟨Ω, hiΩ⟩. The result Mi annihilates Ω, and the Mi add up to H − E0. The positive pieces are ki = |Mi|/c*, with c* a constant that makes ki ≤ 1.

Section 4: cutting an operator B down to a ball. The ball Nl holds every site within graph distance l of a chosen site of term i. All other sites are “out”. Ei,l(B) traces B over the outside sites, drawn as the loop. It then puts back the identity there, divided by its dimension q|out|. Here q is the dimension of one qudit.

stages.title: Replicas trade information against energy
stages.physics: Work with k copies of the state at once. Each copy is Ω̃ beside a maximally entangled pair on two extra registers, C and R. Here Ω̃ is the ground state of the Hamiltonian truncated near the target; it is very close to the true one. Keep one sector of the permutation symmetry of the R registers: {{tn:al-prevector}}. In this formula Bell is the pair on C and R, and πRλk keeps the sector labelled λk. Then apply an inverse power of a positive operator. That operator changes smoothly as a small region moves across a partition. Per copy, the log-norm of the result tends to a combination of entropies. Trees of matrix geometric means organize this averaging.
stages.delivers: The log-norm falls as the small region moves. That fall bounds the conditional mutual information from below. The same states bound the energy the move costs. Two comparisons then pin down the norm. For the upper one, project the target and C onto a maximally entangled pair B: {{tn:al-pin}}. Here d* is the pair's dimension and z the probability kept in the target's typical Schmidt indices. ψ is the typical part of Ω̃, with the target's Schmidt index moved onto R. The lower comparison uses the gap. A low-energy state has most copies in the ground state.
stages.caption: As the number k of copies grows, the log-norm per copy of the filtered state settles at a combination of entropies (dashed). The filtered state is the k-copy state after the positive operator is applied. Comparing this limit with the energy spent bounds the conditional mutual information.

diagrams.caption: Lemma 5.1. θ is a pure state on four parts P, x, U, F. Read left to right; the first filter acts first. First filter x together with U, then x together with P. Each filter first divides by a small power of θ's reduced state on U or P, the hatted ρ. It then multiplies by the same power of any density matrix, τ or σ. The power is a/2. The norm drops by about e−aη/2. Here η is the information x shares with F given U; it equals the same given P. In the error term, ℓ = log(e · dim x) and C is a universal constant.

stages.title: Scan a collar
stages.physics: Sweep a partition across a collar, a band around the target X. The steps follow a finite random schedule. So each interaction term is rarely cut. Repeating the two norm comparisons first improves the box exponent. Then it bounds the information between X and the region beyond the collar. That information is computed in the state {{tn:al-collar}}. This is the ground state Ω with the collar Y traced out.
stages.delivers: The target is X = A ∩ T, where A is one side of the cut. T is a template: a union of small rectangles and triangles of diameter n, with about n boundary edges. Take a collar of width about n1−ε, with ε = 10−5. The mutual information between X and everything beyond the collar is at most C n1−ε, for a constant C.
stages.caption: Five steps of the sweep, drawn side by side. Blue is the target. The partition (orange) crosses the collar (grey) at a different place in each step. A random schedule picks these places. So each interaction term is cut in only a few steps.

diagrams.caption: On the lattice Λ: the target X, the collar Y around it, and the far region beyond. S0 = X ∪ Y is the target with its collar. The scan bounds the mutual information between X and the far region Λ ∖ S0. The bound is C n1−ε (Proposition 9.6). Here n is the target's size, ε = 10−5, and C is a constant.

stages.title: Amplify the information bound
stages.physics: Add two reference copies of the target's sites, s′ and e′. Move the target's state onto e′ and leave the target blank. Typical spectral subspaces give an operator that restores the target, purified by s′. Products of the positive local pieces of the Hamiltonian remove the part of this operator that leaves the ground state. Polar decomposition then turns it into a unitary U′ near the target: {{tn:al-restore}}. Here Ω is the ground state, ρX is the target's reduced state, and triangles are blank states. U′ acts only on s′ and sites near the target. It never touches e′ or the far region. So the target ends up nearly independent of the far region.
stages.delivers: Widen the collar by a sublinear amount. Then the information leaked past it is smaller than any fixed inverse power of n, the target's size.
stages.caption: Information leaked past the collar, against collar width, on a log scale. Here n is the target's size. After the scan, at most C n1−ε leaks, with C a constant and ε = 10−5. Widening the collar by a sublinear amount drives the leak below n−M, for any fixed M.

diagrams.caption: From Section 10. X is the target, and S0 is X with its collar. The outer square holds every site within graph distance 2r of S0, with r sublinear in the target's size. The restoring unitary U′ acts only there and on a reference copy s′ of the target. Everything outside is untouched. So the target's information with it becomes tiny.

From Section 10. Each positive local piece ki annihilates the ground state, and their sum has a gap g. Give each piece a clock that rings at random, at rate one, for a time t. Each ring applies the contraction Gi = (I − ki)1/2. D is the product in ringing order. It leaves the ground state alone. On average it shrinks the squared norm of the rest of any vector by e−gt. Keeping only rings near the target, with truncated pieces, makes the product local.

stages.title: Arrange regions so the entropies cancel
stages.physics: Remove a set D of sites from A. It has at most a constant times as many sites as A has boundary edges. Split the rest of A into regions sorted into two ordered families. A collar keeps each region away from the outside of A. It also keeps it away from the earlier regions of its own family. The ground state ψ is pure, so complementary parts share their nonzero spectrum: {{tn:al-purity}}. Here B is the outside of A, Af is one family, and A1−f is the other. Narrow strips and repeated repairs at point contacts handle any cut, even domains with holes.
stages.delivers: Apply the entropy chain rule once per family. Every region's entropy cancels. What is left is S(A) ≤ |D| log q plus small errors, with q the qudit dimension. The errors add up to at most a constant times the boundary of A. This is the area law.

diagrams.caption: Lemma 11.1 on the lattice. Inside the region A sit the removed layer D and the regions X1, X2, X3. X1 and X3 form one family, X2 the other. B is everything outside A. Each region is nearly independent of B plus the earlier regions of its own family. Two chain rules then cancel every region's entropy. This leaves S(A) ≤ |D| log q plus small errors, with q the qudit dimension.

routes.heading: How the PEPS is built
routes.intro: The construction distributes the ground state among parties, one for each dyadic square, until every site has its own party. Parties may act arbitrarily on what they hold, and each interacts with boundedly many others over its lifetime. Compressing the shared resources gives polynomial bonds, and routing the links places them on the original grid.

stages.title: Information fades with angular separation
stages.physics: Two regions are almost independent when a buffer separates them well. The buffer may narrow linearly toward finitely many points. But its width must stay above a large multiple of log L, where L is the grid side. The proof adds cells one at a time. It uses the two ordered families of regions from the area-law proof. Gaussian filtering in energy, using the gap, resets the information cost after each step inward.
stages.delivers: Their mutual information is at most L−p, for any fixed p. Now split the lattice into a region T, a buffer U and the rest E. Suppose one party holds U. It can apply an isometry V that splits the ground state Ω into a product: {{tn:peps-split}}. Here s holds T and one output of V, and s′ holds E and the other. The error is at most √I(T : E).
stages.caption: Two regions X and E, separated by a buffer. The buffer narrows linearly toward a point. Its width never drops below K log L, with L the grid side and K a large constant. Then X and E are almost independent. Their mutual information is at most L−p, for a fixed p.

diagrams.caption: The partition used in Lemma 6.4: a region T, a buffer U held by one party, and the rest E. Suppose T and E are almost independent. Then the buffer's owner can split its share in two. One part goes with T, the other with E.

stages.title: Small patches with polynomial rank
stages.physics: Pick a square of side about log L, where L is the grid side. Near it, the ground state lies almost entirely in a sum of orthogonal subspaces. Each subspace is spanned by a few vectors on a nested square, times everything outside that square. The square may differ between subspaces. The proof combines nested filters, the gap and the area law. It needs no sharp cut at one fixed boundary.
stages.delivers: The numbers dj of vectors in the subspaces add up to at most C Lc, for constants C and c. An encoder K acts on a square Q+ around the patch, called a hole. It writes which subspace and which vector into a small register 𝒥. It replaces that vector by a fixed product state. Applied to the ground state Ω, it gives the encoded state Ω𝓕: {{tn:peps-encode}}.
stages.caption: Left: nested squares around a square of side about log L, with L the grid side. Right: one bar per subspace j, as tall as its number of vectors dj. The total is at most C Lc, polynomial in L. So the label of a subspace and vector fits in a small register.

diagrams.caption: Around a centre c lie two squares of half-widths h and 2h: Q−(c, h) inside and Q+(c, h) outside (drawn with h = 2). Proposition 4.1 picks nested squares Dj, one per subspace j. Each Dj lies between the two squares, and its size may vary with j. The encoder acts on Q+ only.

stages.title: Local moves on frames
stages.physics: A frame records which party owns each site. It also records which small squares are stored in encoded form. Three moves change a frame. One changes the owner of a region. One creates or retires a party. One swaps ownership of a region between two copies of the state. A birth uses one normalized pair state {{tn:peps-pair}}. Here s lives on the region T and an extra register 𝓑T. The old owner first projects onto s privately. It then prepares a fresh copy of s whose T half goes to the new party. Everything else is a private map of one party.
stages.delivers: Each move changes the ideal state by at most a constant times L−20, with L the grid side. Births and swaps cost at most a constant times L−30. These errors are small enough to sum over the whole protocol.

diagrams.caption: Lemma 6.5, read left to right. One party owns a region T and a buffer U; E is the rest. It applies an isometry V to U, giving registers 𝓑T and 𝓑E. It projects T and 𝓑T onto a normalized state s. It then prepares a fresh |s⟩, whose T half belongs to the new party. Finally V† recombines the registers. If T and E are almost independent, the error is at most L−30, with L the grid side.

Lemma 6.6. Two copies of the state, labelled (1) and (2), swap who owns a region T. Only private operations are used. In each copy, the owner of the buffer U applies an isometry V. This splits off a register 𝓑T that belongs with T. The T and 𝓑T parts are swapped between the copies. Then V† recombines. If the split were exact, the swap would change nothing. So the error is at most 4L−30, with L the grid side.

Lemma 6.3: re-encoding a small patch. Kold† undoes the old encoding of the square Q+ and reads its tag register 𝒥old. Projections P1, …, Pm onto low-rank subspaces of m nearby patches follow. Knew writes the new encoding and its tag 𝒥new. The error is at most (m + rold)ε. Here rold counts the old encoded squares that change, and ε = L−60, with L the grid side.

stages.title: A dyadic distribution protocol
stages.physics: One party starts with the whole ground state Ω. Ownership passes down a hierarchy of dyadic squares, halving the side at each step. It stops when every site has its own party. Extra copies of Ω supply the surroundings that each change of owner needs.
stages.delivers: Every party takes part in boundedly many operations with other parties, at two adjacent scales.
stages.caption: The hierarchy, drawn side by side, from one party to one party per site. In each panel the outlined square is a parent. Its children (blue) are the parties it works with at the next scale.

stages.title: Compress the shared resources
stages.physics: The protocol uses shared pair states of unbounded Schmidt rank. The proof then computes the output density matrix. In it, each pair-state operator |η⟩⟨η̃| is replaced by a random sum of k product terms: {{tn:peps-source}}. Here Uj and Vj are random Gaussian factors on the two halves, and 𝔼 is the average. The sum equals the original on average. The number k is polynomial in the grid side L. Each party joins only boundedly many operations, which keeps the coefficients small. A Gaussian second-moment bound controls the error.
stages.delivers: The trace-norm error does not depend on any private dimension. The result is an operator network with one node per party. Its bonds have dimension polynomial in the grid side.

stages.title: Back to a vector on the grid
stages.physics: The compressed network describes an operator. Fix each of its input legs to one product basis vector, drawn as a triangle. This leaves a vector network with the same bonds: {{tn:peps-column}}. Here σ is the operator tensor at each party and v the resulting vector tensor. Some such choice is close to the ground state Ω. Links join parties at nearby dyadic scales. Route each link along a row, then a column. Then each lattice edge carries boundedly many links.
stages.delivers: The result is a PEPS {{tn:peps-sheet}}: one tensor per site of the original L×L grid, joined along grid edges. Its bond dimension is at most C Lc, for constants C and c. Its normalized error is at most 1/L.
stages.caption: The links between parents and children on an 8 × 8 grid, routed first along a row and then along a column. Stroke width counts the links that share each lattice edge, which sets the bond dimension there.

diagrams.caption: Lemma 8.2 on a small grid. The parent party Q and its four children P sit at fixed centre sites of their dyadic squares. Each link (red) runs along a row and then a column. At each site it passes, it carries an identity tensor. All link indices crossing a grid edge are grouped into one bond. Each edge carries boundedly many links, so every bond has polynomial dimension.

stages.title: Models and conventions
stages.physics: Both proofs share the same definitions. Hamiltonians live on finite lattice domains, possibly with holes. Regions have reduced states and entropies. The global gap is restated as an energy inequality. The papers' PEPS has one tensor Av per site v: {{tn:peps-tensor}}. It matches the tensor networks of TNLean exactly.
stages.delivers: Lean statements of both main theorems with no hypothesis the papers lack.
stages.caption: A finite domain Λ of the square lattice, with a hole and an irregular edge. The blue sites form a region A. The orange edges join A to the rest of Λ; together they form ∂ΛA. The area law bounds the entropy of A by a constant times their number.

glossary: S(A) = −Tr ρ<sub>A</sub> log ρ<sub>A</sub> for the reduced state of region A. It measures how entangled A is with the rest of the system.
I(B:C) = S(B) + S(C) − S(B∪C), the total correlation between B and C. Small I means B and C are nearly independent.
A buffer zone of chosen width around a region. The area-law proof shows that almost no information crosses a collar of slightly sublinear width.
The energy gap Δ of the full Hamiltonian above its unique ground state. No gap is assumed for any subregion.
A state built by contracting one tensor per site along the lattice edges. The bond dimension D is the size of each contracted index.
Many copies of the ground state taken together. The argument works in their symmetric subspace and then lets the number of copies grow.
